READING

**The numbers as they stand**

The upfront cost gap between the two courses is GBP 950,000 in TARNSIDE's favour (GBP 1,730,000 versus GBP 2,680,000). That is not trivial, but it is the entire financial argument for TARNSIDE. Every other financial variable runs the other way.

The GBP 190,000 annual fuel saving in VELLACOTT's favour produces a break-even on that GBP 950,000 premium in exactly five years, with no discounting. Add the residual value of the two assets at that point — a 2017 hull at fourteen years old versus a re-engined 1995 hull at thirty-six years old — and the real crossover is closer to three or four years. Beyond that crossover, TARNSIDE is the more expensive choice every year in perpetuity as long as the route continues, and the gap compounds.

Kittiwake's GBP 610,000 valuation on the Brindlemere is in the same order of magnitude as a scrapping or distressed-sale price for a 31-year-old ferry, not a premium secondhand price. That figure will not improve as the hull ages further. If TARNSIDE is chosen, that asset walks off the balance sheet in value over the following decade. Under VELLACOTT, the GBP 610,000 is realised now and the replacement asset is a nine-year-old vessel that will hold value for twenty or more years.

**The twelve-week yard period**

TARNSIDE requires the Brindlemere to go to Hebridean & Vaile for twelve weeks from 5 January 2027. The Sorrelbank charter covers the service, and GBP 310,000 has been allowed for it. But a charter vessel introduces four risks that are not priced: (1) any cost overrun in the yard, (2) any additional day-rate or mobilisation charge if the charter period extends, (3) the possibility that a relief vessel of a different ramp geometry or passenger arrangement creates handling difficulties at Kettlebay or Ardvraich, and (4) the reputational effect on regular customers of a substitution during twelve weeks that includes the Easter period and the run-up to summer. January to April is off-peak, but Easter 2027 falls within that window (Good Friday is 2 April). These are not show-stoppers but they are uncosted.

VELLACOTT has no yard period. The Suilvenaig is on the water and earns from handover.

**Hull age**

This is, in my view, the single most important consideration that the headline figures do not fully capture. The Brindlemere's hull passed its March 2026 survey with no steelwork required, which is genuinely good news for a 31-year-old vessel. But the surveyor's endorsement means "acceptable today," not "good for another decade." Steelwork bills on ageing hulls do not announce themselves in advance. By re-engining, you are committing GBP 1,420,000 of capital to a vessel that will be 32 years old at completion and whose hull costs are structurally unpredictable from roughly 2029 onwards. The new engines will be warranted; the hull will not.

The Suilvenaig at nine years old is in mid-life. Her hull should be straightforward to survey and insure. She was designed and built to modern standards — fuel economy, emissions, ramp geometry — and those advantages will become more material, not less, as environmental regulation on coastal services tightens.

**Master rota**

VELLACOTT reduces the active master rota from nine to seven. That is a 22% reduction in rostering flexibility for a year-round, single-vessel service running up to eleven crossings a day. In summer this will be tight. The seven remaining masters will also each need to complete the six-week endorsement before they can sail the Suilvenaig; the cost of those courses is not in the figures given and should be established, but six courses for seven people staggered over the autumn and winter of 2026–27 is achievable without leaving the vessel short at any one time.

The two masters who have said they will retire rather than sit the course are a real loss. Whether they can be replaced with qualified endorsement-holders is the question Ingrid needs to answer before committing to VELLACOTT, and it should be answerable within weeks — the maritime labour market in this region is not opaque. If replacement masters with the right endorsement can be recruited, the rota concern disappears. If they cannot, then running seven-handed through the 2027 summer season with no slack is a genuine operational risk.

TARNSIDE avoids this entirely. All nine masters remain, no training requirement changes, the rota is unchanged.

**Insurance — the critical unknown**

The broker has not yet quoted on the Suilvenaig. This is the most significant open variable in the analysis. It could break in either direction: a newer, better-built vessel might attract lower premiums; a vessel requiring crew endorsements that some of your masters currently lack might attract a loading. If the annual premium differential is, say, GBP 50,000 in VELLACOTT's disfavour, the payback period on the upfront premium extends from five years to roughly six and a half — still clearly favourable. If the differential were GBP 100,000 a year, payback stretches to around twelve years — still positive, but into territory where the comparison becomes genuinely uncertain. Only at a differential of around GBP 190,000 a year or more would VELLACOTT lose its financial advantage entirely, and that would be an extraordinary loading on a nine-year-old vessel.

This quote must be obtained before contracts are exchanged. It is not a reason to abandon VELLACOTT; it is a reason not to sign anything until the broker has reported.

**Timing**

The Brindlemere valuation is held until 2027-02-11 and the Suilvenaig is available from 2026-11-20. If VELLACOTT is the chosen course, there is a clear path: get the insurance quote now, get the master recruitment picture clear by October, exchange on the Suilvenaig in November, and sell the Brindlemere before the valuation expires in February. The linkspan work at Ardvraich can run through the winter alongside any master training. None of this is a rushed timetable.

**Summary of the decision**

TARNSIDE is the lower-risk, lower-complexity option. It is right to name that clearly. But the risks it avoids are procedural (training, endorsements, linkspan) rather than existential, and most of them are temporary. The costs it imposes — higher fuel bill in perpetuity, ongoing decline of a 1995 hull, the certain loss of the GBP 610,000 sale value as the vessel ages further — are permanent.

VELLACOTT's risks are concentrated and resolvable: get the insurance quote, clarify master recruitment, verify the linkspan programme. If those three things come back acceptably, VELLACOTT is the stronger position financially within five years and the only sustainable long-term asset strategy.

CALL
  VELLACOTT

GROUNDS
  The GBP 950,000 upfront premium is recovered within five years from fuel savings alone, and the differential in hull age and long-run asset value makes VELLACOTT the sounder position for every subsequent year of the service's operation — subject only to the insurance quote, which must be obtained before committing.
